---
title: "R reference for analytical measurements"
---

## Start in the supplied project

Extract [the course project](../downloads/analyticalchem-project.zip), open
`analyticalchem.Rproj`, and keep `course-report.Rmd` at the project root. Install
missing packages once in the R console:

```{r}
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
```

Read a lesson's code from top to bottom in a fresh session. Run R in the R console,
not a shell terminal. Keep raw CSV files unchanged. Units and row meanings are
specified in the [course data dictionary](data.qmd).

## Inspect before calculating

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
x <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(x)
names(x)
head(x)
sum(is.na(x$chloride_mg_l))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(x$sample_id))
```

`stopifnot()` stops the script if its condition is false. Here it prevents
mistaking duplicate IDs for independent collected samples. A failed check
calls for inspection; it is not a command to delete rows automatically.

## Calculate and summarise

```{r}
x <- x |> mutate(chloride_mg = chloride_mg_l * collected_l)
x |> group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(chloride_mg_l), .groups = "drop")
```

`|>` passes a result to the next function. `mutate()` adds derived columns.
`group_by()` identifies groups for `summarise()`. Describe how missing values
are handled and count them; `na.rm = TRUE` does not justify ignoring missingness.

## Attach a preparation by ID

```r
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(preparations$preparation_id),
          all(readings$preparation_id %in% preparations$preparation_id))
joined <- readings |>
  left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")
```

This example assumes the two tables have been imported in the relevant lesson.
`left_join()` uses matching IDs, not row position. Unique preparation keys avoid
multiplying rows; checking matches avoids losing the volume or mass needed for
a calculation. Inspect row count and missing values afterwards.

## Fit a line and respect its direction

```r
fit <- lm(response ~ known_concentration, data = standards)
coef(fit)
residuals(fit)
```

The response is on the left. An inverse concentration estimate uses the fitted
response relationship; fitting the variables in the opposite direction is a
different regression. Inspect residuals, range and QC before exporting results.

## Logarithms and differences

```{r}
log10(0.0001)
10^(-4)
diff(c(0, 1, 1.5, 2))
```

`log10()` gives a base-ten logarithm; `10^x` reverses it. The logarithm of a
physical quantity is taken relative to a stated reference/unit convention.
`diff()` gives consecutive differences. A titration derivative divides the pH
differences by the corresponding volume differences, not by the number of rows.

## Save the evidence

```{r}
fig <- ggplot(x, aes(location, chloride_mg_l)) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Sampling location", y = "Chloride (mg/L)") + theme_minimal()
ggsave("output/water-plot.png", plot = fig, width = 7, height = 4)
write_csv(x, "output/water-results.csv")
```

Keep the source report at the root. Render from the console, outside the report:

```r
rmarkdown::render("course-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
```

An object-not-found error can mean a misspelling or a missing earlier step.
A file-not-found error usually calls for checking project, relative path and
filename. If Knit fails while Console succeeds, check for hidden session state.
Restart R and rebuild from saved inputs rather than manually repairing the HTML.
